question: In recent years, the exposure of minors to social media has become an increasingly serious issue with regard to public health, the protection of minors and digital safety. Algorithms that favour engaging content, extensive data collection and addiction-inducing mechanisms can amplify the risks to child and teen development through exposure to harmful content, online harassment, manipulation and social pressure.
For these worrying reasons, which are having an ever greater impact on our daily lives, the Union should act quicker to protect minors and establish clear rules on social media access for minors.

I would like to ask the Commission to clarify whether it intends to put forward a unified European legislative framework that would include setting an EU-wide common minimum age, to ensure children are equally protected across all Member States and to strengthen platform responsibility with regard to compliance with these rules.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.11.2026) On 17 September 2026, the Commission adopted the proposal for an EU KIDS Act –‘EU Keeping Internet Digital Spaces Accountable and Trustworthy’1 to enhance the online safety of children and ensure an equal level of protection throughout the EU.

The proposal builds upon the recommendations of the report of the co-chairs of the Special Panel on Child Safety Online, presented in July 2026, adopting a developmental approach that ensures that children’s online experiences and protections should grow with their age. The EU KIDS Act has one clear goal: making the online experience for children age-appropriate and safe by design.

Children should enter the online world in a gradual manner. Starting from 13, minors will be able to use special accounts on social networking and video-sharing platforms set up by their guardians, with additional safeguards. As of 15, minors will be able to autonomously enter the digital world by setting up their own account.

All services in scope are required to instate effective safety-by-design measures, such as disabling addictive design features, ensuring high privacy settings for minors’ accounts, adapting algorithms to prevent exposure to harmful content, and instating effective and easy to use parental controls.

To ensure effective and robust enforcement, the proposal builds upon the existing enforcement architectures under the Digital Services Act2 and AI Act3 and introduces a fast-track 90-day enforcement procedure. Providers covered by the EU KIDS Act that have been designated as very large online platforms under the DSA are also required to submit an audited compliance plan.
